I faced this issue today on my OpenCode Desktop Beta:


```
Could not reach Local Server
Retrying automatically...
```

How to fix?

I have been thinking about a related problem: once agents can coordinate as a team, "agent memory" should probably be more than a per-agent blob. The useful unit is often an experience: under which task condition, which action or route worked, which route failed, and whether the lesson is reusable by other agents.

I built a small free and open-source tool called Khaos Brain for that reason. It is a local-first experience system for AI agents.

Khaos Brain stores experience as visible file-based cards instead of opaque memory. The cards are inspectable, searchable, reviewable, Git-versionable, and can be merged or rolled back. It also separates personal/local preferences from reusable team or organization knowledge.

For this DB-backed team coordination proposal, I think the interesting overlap is the `agent_memory` table. One possible design question is whether memory should only be "agent X remembers Y", or whether some memories should become reviewed team experience:

- task condition
- route/action taken
- result
- failed alternative
- better route
- skill dependency
- local-only vs team-shareable

Repo:
https://github.com/liuyingxuvka/Khaos-Brain

Feedback:
https://github.com/liuyingxuvka/Khaos-Brain/discussions/2

If useful, Khaos Brain may be a reference point for the memory/experience layer around team agents, even if your runtime state itself remains DB-backed.

I found a temporary workaround for the current behavior by using an opencode hook to inject my PowerShell profile before every agent `bash` tool execution.

```js
// .opencode/plugins/source-before-bash.js
export const SourceBeforeBash = async () => {
  return {
    "tool.execute.before": async (input, output) => {
      if (input.tool !== "bash") return

      const command = output.args?.command
      if (!command || typeof command !== "string") return

      const sourceFile = "C:/Users/<Username>/Documents/PowerShell/Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1"

      if (command.includes("$env:__BASH_AUTO_INJECT")) return

      output.args.command =
        `. '${sourceFile}'; $env:__BASH_AUTO_INJECT = 1; ${command}`
    },
  }
}
````

This makes the agent `bash` tool load the same profile initialization that I expect in my normal shell session, so aliases/functions/PATH changes from my PowerShell profile become available to agent-executed commands as well.

The `$env:__BASH_AUTO_INJECT = 1` marker is necessary as a sentinel. It prevents the hook from injecting the same source command repeatedly if a command is already wrapped. It also helps when the injected command leaks into the visible tool history and the agent later copies or imitates the previous command: the hook can detect the marker and avoid a second injection. Without this guard, commands can become nested like:

```powershell
. 'profile.ps1'; . 'profile.ps1'; . 'profile.ps1'; <actual command>
```

This workaround is functional, but it has two drawbacks:

1. The injected prefix is currently visible in the command shown to the user and/or retained in the agent-visible history.
2. That increases token usage and can encourage the agent to learn or reproduce implementation details that should ideally remain a transport/runtime concern.

This is very close to the motivation behind #5321, where `displayInput` would allow a plugin to execute a wrapped command while displaying the original, unwrapped command. I agree with that direction. The hook/plugin layer would be much safer and cleaner if opencode officially supported a way for `tool.execute.before` hooks to distinguish between:

* the command actually executed by the runtime, and
* the command shown in the UI / persisted into agent-visible history.

Related work also appears in #6927, which mentions #5321 as related to tool input/output display behavior.

So while this hook is a usable temporary workaround, I would still prefer an official solution that either:

* unifies shell initialization between user `!` shell and agent `bash` tool directly, or
* provides a documented hook/display API so wrappers can safely hide injected runtime prefixes.

This would improve security, reduce token usage, and avoid training the agent to copy internal wrapper commands.

  -w "/work$(pwd)" \
  -v "$HOME/.local/share/opencode:/root/.local/share/opencode:Z" \
  -v "$HOME/.local/state/opencode:/root/.local/state/opencode:Z" \
  -v "$HOME/.config/opencode:/root/.config/opencode:Z" \
  -v "$HOME/.cache/opencode:/root/.cache/opencode:Z" \
  --network host \
  --volume /tmp/.X11-unix:/tmp/.X11-unix:ro \
  --volume $HOME/.Xauthority:/root/.Xauthority:ro \
  --env DISPLAY=$DISPLAY \
  ghcr.io/randommm/opencode

Hi @Hona, thanks for the quick response. I understand that shell-in-shell execution is a common bypass, but I’d like to push back a bit on framing this as _expected behavior_.

The core issue here is not only that WSL can invoke `powershell.exe` from `bash`; it is that OpenCode’s own safety contract appears to have failed. The system prompt tells the agent:

> “You should not ask permission to use the tool; the user will be presented with a confirmation dialogue upon use.”

In my WSL environment, that dialogue was **never shown**. The agent modified Windows registry keys and force-killed Explorer with zero user interaction. To me, the bug is not merely the shell-in-shell bypass, but the lack of a safe fallback when the confirmation UI does not appear.

The agent's decision boundary was also questionable. I merely asked about an error message. Why would the agent unilaterally decide to modify registry keys and restart Explorer instead of explaining the error message first? Even if the confirmation UI had worked, this level of autonomous action warrants a conversation, not silent execution. Is there any safeguard on _what_ the agent chooses to do, independent of the confirmation mechanism?

I also think relying on users to manually deny-list commands like `powershell.exe`, `cmd.exe`, or `reg.exe` does not scale well, especially because many WSL users may not realize this risk exists. The default state should fail safe, not silently execute.

A reasonable fix might be: if the confirmation dialogue cannot be rendered or intercepted correctly, abort the tool call and surface an error instead of proceeding. Alternatively, OpenCode could document this limitation much more explicitly and provide a default WSL-safe permission profile.

I’m okay if this is considered a known limitation of the current permission model, but closing it as simply “expected” seems to understate the user-safety issue: the agent was told that the user would get a confirmation dialogue, while the user in fact got none.
